The FOMC’s September 2018 statement describes a robust macro backdrop—strong job gains, low unemployment, and inflation near 2%—and pairs it with a 25 bp hike and guidance for “further gradual increases.” This reaction function is consistent with Taylor-rule style behavior highlighted in the academic literature, where policy rates respond positively to activity above potential and inflation near/above target (e.g., rule-like behavior and the Taylor principle). The Committee’s note that longer-term inflation expectations are “little changed” is consistent with expectations/anchoring and sticky-information insights (e.g., Mankiw and Reis), while the choice of gradualism reflects interest-rate smoothing documented in the literature (Goodfriend; Fuhrer). Given tight labor markets, Phillips-curve and labor-market-frictions work (Blanchard-Gali; Ravenna-Walsh) supports vigilance but not urgency when inflation is near target, aligning with the Committee’s “balanced risks” language. Overall, the tone is confident and mildly hawkish, grounded in well-established policy frameworks.
